analysis.one_liner: Guarantees college athletes the right to earn money from their name, image, and likeness under FTC oversight.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2022 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, but never got a hearing or a vote before the 117th Congress ended; it had no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write national rules for college athletes' name, image, and likeness (NIL) deals. It would guarantee athletes the right to market themselves and hire an agent, let them transfer schools once without losing eligibility or scholarships, and require agents to report NIL payments to schools. At the same time, it would declare that athletes are not employees of their schools, bar schools and athletic associations from paying athletes directly, and wipe out state laws that already regulate NIL — leaving the National Collegiate Athletic Association's amateur model in place while trimming some of its control.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes would gain a federal guarantee they can earn money from sponsorships and endorsements, keep their scholarships regardless of NIL earnings, use certified agents, rescind long-term NIL deals they signed while playing, and transfer once without penalty. The federal framework would also give brands and agents one clear national rulebook instead of a patchwork of state laws.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires athletic associations, conferences, and schools to let athletes market their name, image, or likeness for pay and to retain a certified agent for NIL matters.
It bars schools from revoking or reducing an athlete's scholarship because the athlete earned NIL compensation, and limits transfer penalties to one penalty-free transfer with advance notice.

It would create an FTC Office of Sport to certify agents, hear complaints, and enforce the rules, and require a Government Accountability Office report on athlete health insurance and scholarship needs.
It requires third parties to get written consent from every team member before using a group's name, image, or likeness, protecting athletes from group deals they did not agree to.

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA, conferences, and universities would lose some control over their athletes' commercial activity, and boosters would be barred from using NIL money to recruit players. Athletes would also give something up: the bill declares them not employees, forecloses school-paid compensation, and overrides state laws that had given athletes rights on their own terms.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that a student athlete 'shall not be considered an employee' of their school or athletic association for playing their sport, which would lock in amateur status and shut the door to employment-based pay, union representation, and labor-law claims that courts were actively considering.

The bill preempts state laws governing athlete compensation and eligibility, erasing protections states such as California had already enacted and replacing them with this federal standard, which is narrower in some respects.

The bill gives schools, conferences, and athletic associations immunity from liability for having prohibited athletes from being paid before enactment, and leaves associations free to keep banning pay-for-play, entrenching the existing amateur model rather than dismantling it.
Enforcement runs through a new FTC Office of Sport that would set agent standards and booster limits, an unfamiliar regulatory role for the agency and a new layer between athletes and their earnings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers athletes real, concrete gains — a federal right to earn NIL money, scholarship protection, one free transfer, and certified agents — which matters in a world where the NCAA had long restricted athletes' earnings while schools and broadcasters profited. But it is a bargain struck in the NCAA's favor: athletes get commercial rights while expressly remaining non-employees, schools remain barred from paying them, and state laws are swept aside. Someone who believes athletes in a billion-dollar enterprise are performing work and deserve employment rights would see this bill as codifying the old model with a few new freedoms attached.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Wicker introduced the bill in September 2022 and it went straight to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it; when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, the bill died there.

narrative.text: Senator Roger Wicker of Mississippi, the top Republican on the Senate Commerce Committee, introduced the bill on September 14, 2022.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action was ever taken on it.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill lapsed in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the status quo held: the NCAA and universities continued operating under the state-by-state NIL patchwork and their own interim rules without a federal standard. Athletes kept whatever rights their states gave them, but got none of the federal guarantees, transfer relief, or agent protections the bill would have provided — and the question of whether college athletes are employees remained unresolved.

for.name: Sen. Roger Wicker
for.role: U.S. Senator from Mississippi; ranking Republican on the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the Collegiate Athlete Compensation Rights Act on September 14, 2022.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, and no vote, leaving the bill to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate colleagues
against.what_they_did: None added their names as cosponsors before the bill lapsed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and the Democratic-led committee that held it never took it up, so no meaningful party split ever formed.

industries.industry: NCAA, athletic conferences, and university athletic departments
industries.note: The bill strips these bodies of their power to block athletes' individual NIL earnings, but locks in the core of their amateur model: athletes are declared non-employees, schools and associations remain barred from paying them, and the associations keep their rulemaking and enforcement role. It also grants them immunity for their past NIL bans.

The bill formally recognizes booster-funded NIL deals as the channel for athlete payments but bans boosters from conditioning or offering NIL money to induce an athlete to enroll at or transfer to a school, curbing the recruiting-warfare side of the business. If boosters profit by luring athletes with pay-for-play arrangements, that interest runs against the schools' competitive balance and athletes' educational stability.

industries.industry: Sports agents and athlete marketing firms
industries.note: The bill makes agent certification mandatory through the FTC, creating a licensed, regulated market for NIL representation. Athletes benefit from a vetted-agent system, and agents gain a protected franchise in it.

industries.industry: Brands and media companies that license college sports
industries.note: Marketers gain a single national rulebook instead of conflicting state NIL laws, but must obtain written consent from every team member for group uses and report deal terms. Broadcast partners keep their carve-out to use athletes' images in game coverage without paying them individually.

industries.industry: Gambling, tobacco, alcohol, and adult entertainment
industries.note: The bill lets schools and associations bar athletes from NIL deals promoting these products, keeping a category of endorsement money off the table.
